krakatoa.title: Iceland’s Laki eruption
krakatoa.line: Laki erupted for eight months; its sulfur haze sickened Europe and chilled the Northern Hemisphere, and famine killed a fifth of Icelanders.

krakatoa.title: Mount Tambora erupts in Indonesia
krakatoa.line: Tambora, the largest eruption in recorded history, killed tens of thousands and brought 1816’s “Year Without a Summer” to Europe and America.

krakatoa.title: Mount Pinatubo erupts in the Philippines
krakatoa.line: The 20th century’s second-largest eruption lofted about 15 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide and cooled the planet by about 0.5°C.

scramble.title: The Dutch seize Elmina Castle
scramble.line: The Dutch seized Portugal’s Elmina Castle in today’s Ghana as European rivals fought over forts for the gold and slave trades.

scramble.title: The Congo Crisis
scramble.line: As Congo won independence, Belgium, the US, the Soviet Union and the UN intervened, making it a Cold War battleground.

scramble.title: Angola becomes a Cold War battlefield
scramble.line: At Angola’s independence, Cuban troops and Soviet arms backed one side while the US and South Africa backed its rivals.

trusts.title: England’s Statute of Monopolies
trusts.line: England’s Parliament voided most royal grants of monopoly over everyday trades, but allowed patents for new inventions.

trusts.title: The breakup of AT&T’s Bell System
trusts.line: To settle a federal antitrust suit, AT&T, which ran most US phone service, split off seven regional “Baby Bells.”

trusts.title: The US sues Microsoft
trusts.line: The US accused Microsoft of using Windows to crush rivals like Netscape; a 2000 breakup order was overturned on appeal.

yellow.title: The Simon of Trent blood libel
yellow.line: After a boy died in Trent, printed accounts spread a false claim that local Jews killed him, among print’s first viral lies.

yellow.title: The Great Moon Hoax
yellow.line: The New York Sun, a cheap new penny paper, claimed astronomers had spotted bat-winged people on the Moon, and its sales soared.

yellow.title: The War of the Worlds broadcast
yellow.line: Orson Welles’s radio drama of a Martian invasion fooled some listeners, and newspapers then spread exaggerated tales of nationwide panic.

yellow.title: India’s WhatsApp rumor lynchings
yellow.line: False WhatsApp rumors of child kidnappers spread among India’s new smartphone users, and mobs killed more than a dozen innocent people.

dreadnought.title: Rome builds a fleet against Carthage
dreadnought.line: Rome, a land power, copied a captured Carthaginian warship, built about 100 in two months, and beat Carthage’s navy at Mylae.

dreadnought.title: The First Anglo-Dutch War
dreadnought.line: England’s growing navy and trade laws aimed at Dutch shipping sparked war with the Dutch Republic, Europe’s leading sea power.

dreadnought.title: The Washington Naval Treaty
dreadnought.line: Facing a costly race, Britain, the US and Japan capped battleships at a 5:5:3 ratio, with Britain accepting parity with America.

ellis.title: The Goths cross the Danube
ellis.line: Fleeing the Huns, tens of thousands of Goths entered the Roman Empire; abuse by officials sparked a revolt that killed Emperor Valens.

ellis.title: Ireland’s famine exodus
ellis.line: Fleeing the Great Famine, over a million Irish emigrated, many to America, where the anti-Catholic Know-Nothing movement surged in the 1850s.

ellis.title: The Chinese Exclusion Act
ellis.line: After Chinese workers came for gold mines and railroads, Congress banned Chinese laborers, the first major US law to bar one nationality.

ellis.title: The Empire Windrush reaches Britain
ellis.line: The Empire Windrush brought Caribbean migrants to postwar Britain; as more followed, riots erupted in 1958 and entry laws tightened from 1962.

modelt.title: The Rover safety bicycle
modelt.line: Starley’s chain-driven Rover replaced the risky high-wheeler, and cheap safety bicycles set off a worldwide cycling craze in the 1890s.

modelt.title: The Volkswagen Beetle goes global
modelt.line: After World War II, Volkswagen mass-produced the Beetle for ordinary buyers; in 1972 it passed the Model T’s production record.

modelt.title: Honda’s Super Cub motorbike
modelt.line: Honda’s cheap, easy-to-ride Super Cub put millions on motorized wheels; over 100 million built make it the best-selling motor vehicle ever.

titanic.title: The warship Vasa sinks
titanic.line: Sweden’s king demanded a mighty showpiece warship, but the top-heavy Vasa capsized less than a mile into its maiden voyage.

titanic.title: The Hindenburg disaster
titanic.line: The hydrogen-filled luxury airship burst into flames while landing in New Jersey, killing 36 and ending the era of passenger airships.

titanic.title: The Concorde crash near Paris
titanic.line: The supersonic jet for wealthy travelers, with a spotless safety record, crashed after takeoff from Paris, killing 113; Concorde retired in 2003.

somme.title: The Siege of Petersburg
somme.line: Union and Confederate armies faced off in trenches around Petersburg for nine months, with mortars, mines and repeating rifles foreshadowing 1916.

somme.title: The Siege of Port Arthur
somme.line: Japanese troops stormed Russian forts through barbed wire and machine-gun fire, losing tens of thousands in a preview of World War I.

somme.title: The Iran–Iraq War
somme.line: Iran and Iraq fought eight years of World War I-style trench warfare, with human-wave attacks, poison gas and missiles fired at cities.

sykes.title: The First Partition of Poland
sykes.line: Russia, Prussia and Austria seized about a third of Poland; Polish insurgents rose against the partitions in 1794, 1830 and 1863.

sykes.title: Britain draws the Durand Line
sykes.line: Britain drew a border splitting Pashtun lands between Afghanistan and British India; Afghanistan never recognized it, and Pashtun fighters defied it.

sykes.title: The Biafran War
sykes.line: Biafra declared independence from Nigeria, a country whose borders Britain had drawn; the war and famine that followed killed perhaps a million.

flu.title: The Plague of Justinian
flu.line: Bubonic plague rode grain ships from Egypt to Constantinople and spread along Mediterranean trade routes, killing millions across the Roman world.

flu.title: The Black Death
flu.line: Plague spread along Silk Road caravans and Genoese trading ships, killing perhaps a third to half of Europe’s people within five years.

flu.title: The 1889 Russian flu
flu.line: Carried by rail and steamship, a new flu swept the Northern Hemisphere in about four months, killing roughly a million people.

flu.title: The 1957 Asian flu
flu.line: A new flu strain from China spread worldwide within months, killing over a million, as labs raced to make vaccines.

weimar.title: The collapse of the Continental dollar
weimar.line: Congress printed Continental dollars to pay for the Revolution until they were nearly worthless, giving rise to “not worth a Continental.”

weimar.title: Hungary’s record hyperinflation
weimar.line: In the worst hyperinflation ever recorded, Hungarian prices doubled about every 15 hours, and a 100 quintillion pengő note was issued.

weimar.title: Zimbabwe’s hyperinflation
weimar.line: Zimbabwe’s central bank printed money until monthly inflation hit about 80 billion percent and a 100 trillion dollar note appeared.
